stem:
A 27-year-old woman (G1P0) presents to your regional maternity unit at 32+1 weeks with 3 hours of regular painful contractions every 4 to 5 minutes. Her pregnancy has been uncomplicated to date. On speculum examination her cervix is 3 cm dilated and 80 percent effaced. Foetal fibronectin is not available in your unit. She has not received any antenatal corticosteroids in this pregnancy.

A foetal ultrasound performed on arrival shows a singleton cephalic presentation with an estimated foetal weight of 1.8 kg on the 45th centile. The CTG shows a baseline of 140/min with normal variability and no decelerations. Blood pressure is normal, urine is clean. There are no signs of chorioamnionitis and membranes are intact.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal pulse 88/min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Cervix 3 cm dilated, 80 percent effaced; membranes intact; foetal head engaged
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 9 x10^9/L; CRP 4 mg/L; urinalysis clear; CTG reassuring

lead_in: What is the most appropriate tocolytic while corticosteroids and neuroprotection are given?

options.text: Oral indomethacin 100 mg loading then 25 mg every 6 hours for a 48 hour course now
options.rationale: Indomethacin risks premature ductal closure and oligohydramnios after 32 weeks; nifedipine is preferred at this gestation. (Source: RANZCOG Preterm labour statement)

options.text: No tocolysis; proceed straight to delivery because dilation is beyond 3 cm
options.rationale: Delay of 48 hours for corticosteroid maturation is beneficial at 32 weeks; tocolysis should be attempted concurrently with steroids. (Source: RANZCOG Preterm labour statement)

options.text: Oral nifedipine 20 mg loading then 20 mg every 30 minutes to a maximum of 40 mg in the first hour
options.rationale: RANZCOG and Australian obstetric protocols use oral nifedipine as first-line tocolytic at 24 to 34 weeks because of maternal tolerability and evidence for 48 hour delay allowing corticosteroids. (Source: RANZCOG Preterm labour statement)

options.text: IV salbutamol infusion at 5 microgram/min titrated to contractions and heart rate
options.rationale: Beta-agonist tocolytics carry unacceptable maternal cardiovascular risk and are second- or third-line only. (Source: RANZCOG Preterm labour statement)

options.text: IV atosiban 6.75 mg bolus then infusion for at least 24 hours as sole tocolytic
options.rationale: Atosiban is effective but more costly and less accessible than nifedipine; it is second-line in Australian practice. (Source: RANZCOG Preterm labour statement)

explanation.summary: Preterm labour management from 24 to 34 weeks aims to buy 48 hours for antenatal corticosteroids (IM betamethasone 11.4 mg two doses 24 hours apart) and to transfer in utero to a facility with appropriate neonatal care. First-line tocolysis in Australia is oral nifedipine; atosiban is second-line where available. Beta-agonists (salbutamol) are avoided due to maternal cardiovascular risk. Indomethacin is avoided after 32 weeks because of premature ductus arteriosus closure and oligohydramnios. Magnesium sulfate is given for neuroprotection when birth is anticipated before 30 weeks (some units extend to 32 weeks).
key_points: Nifedipine oral is first-line tocolytic at 24 to 34 weeks in Australia.
Indomethacin is avoided after 32 weeks for ductal closure risk.
Beta-agonists are avoided for maternal cardiovascular safety.
Magnesium sulfate is used for neuroprotection below 30 weeks (some units to 32 weeks).
explanation.pearls: At 32 weeks in preterm labour give oral nifedipine tocolysis with concurrent IM betamethasone; avoid indomethacin (ductal closure) and beta-agonists (cardiovascular risk).

stem:
A 32-year-old woman (G2P1) attends your antenatal clinic at 36+2 weeks. Her first pregnancy was an uncomplicated term vaginal delivery. On palpation today the foetus feels breech and this is confirmed on point-of-care ultrasound: a frank breech, foetal back on the maternal left, adequate amniotic fluid volume and an anterior placenta clear of the lower segment. Estimated foetal weight is 2.9 kg on the 55th centile.

She has no scars on her uterus, no antepartum haemorrhage in this pregnancy, no known foetal abnormality and no evidence of ruptured membranes. Her booking BMI was 26 kg/m2 and her blood pressure has remained normal throughout. She wants to avoid caesarean if possible and asks about your recommendation for the next 2 weeks.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78/min, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C, foetal heart rate 140/min
data_table.Examination: Symphysio-fundal height 34 cm; frank breech confirmed on point-of-care ultrasound; adequate amniotic fluid; no palpable uterine tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Ultrasound: EFW 2.9 kg (55th centile); anterior placenta clear of lower segment; normal amniotic fluid index

lead_in: What is the most appropriate recommendation now?

options.text: Recommend vaginal breech delivery at 40 weeks without any attempt at ECV as the sole intervention
options.rationale: Vaginal breech is only offered in selected women with strict criteria and experienced operator; ECV is offered first-line. (Source: RANZCOG Management of breech statement)

options.text: Advise moxibustion at the outer little toe alone as the primary intervention until 39 weeks
options.rationale: Moxibustion has limited evidence and is not a substitute for offering ECV in a formal maternity setting. (Source: RANZCOG Management of breech statement)

options.text: Perform ECV in the outpatient clinic today at 36+2 without tocolysis or CTG monitoring
options.rationale: ECV should be performed from 37 weeks in a facility with capacity for immediate caesarean if needed and with CTG monitoring; earlier attempts have higher spontaneous version rates that make procedure unnecessary. (Source: RANZCOG Management of breech statement)

options.text: Offer external cephalic version at 37 weeks with tocolysis and continuous foetal monitoring in the birth suite
options.rationale: RANZCOG recommends ECV from 37 weeks in eligible women with singleton term breech to reduce caesarean rate; her situation has no contraindications. (Source: RANZCOG Management of breech statement)

options.text: Book elective caesarean section for 39 weeks without discussing external cephalic version
options.rationale: ECV should be offered first in eligible women because a successful version returns her to routine cephalic vaginal birth. (Source: RANZCOG Management of breech statement)

explanation.summary: RANZCOG recommends offering external cephalic version from 37 weeks in women with singleton term breech and no contraindications (previous caesarean scar being a relative contraindication, plus antepartum haemorrhage, placenta praevia, oligohydramnios, foetal abnormality, ruptured membranes, multiple pregnancy). ECV is done in a facility with immediate access to caesarean, with tocolysis (typically nifedipine or salbutamol) and continuous CTG. Success rates are 50 to 60 percent in multiparous women and 30 to 40 percent in nulliparous women. Anti-D is given to Rh-negative women within 72 hours of ECV. Vaginal breech delivery is offered only when strict RANZCOG criteria are met with experienced practitioners.
key_points: ECV is first-line for term breech in eligible women.
Performed from 37 weeks with tocolysis and CTG in a birth-ready setting.
Anti-D within 72 hours in Rh-negative women.
Vaginal breech delivery has strict operator and criteria requirements.
explanation.pearls: For a G2P1 with singleton frank breech at 36+2 weeks and no contraindications, offer ECV at 37 weeks with tocolysis and CTG monitoring; anti-D within 72 hours if Rh negative.

stem:
You are the obstetric registrar on-call and are called urgently at 03:15 to a 28-year-old multipara at 39+5 weeks in the birth suite. She has just had spontaneous rupture of membranes with a moderate gush of clear liquor. The midwife immediately palpates a soft pulsatile cord in the vagina at the introitus. The CTG shows a prolonged foetal deceleration to 80/min for the last 3 minutes with poor variability, having previously been reactive.

The patient is a spontaneous labourer with cervix now 6 cm dilated, foetal head at the pelvic inlet, station -2. Full theatre team is stood by and anaesthetist is 8 minutes away by phone. She has been prepared for anaesthesia (fasting 6 hours). She has no significant medical history and no cardiovascular contraindications.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal pulse 100/min, blood pressure 128/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C, foetal heart rate 80/min for 3 minutes
data_table.Examination: Cord palpable and pulsating at introitus; cervix 6 cm dilated; head at -2 station; membranes ruptured
data_table.Investigations: Group and save on file; last Hb 128 g/L (115-160); no pre-existing coagulopathy

lead_in: Which single set of pre-transfer measures should you undertake now to maximise foetal survival before theatre?

options.text: Reduce the cord back through the cervix with a warm saline soaked pack and continue augmentation of labour with routine outpatient follow-up
options.rationale: Cord replacement is not routine; it risks cord damage and delays delivery. (Source: RANZCOG Umbilical cord prolapse statement)

options.text: Continue oxytocin augmentation to achieve rapid vaginal delivery of the head while she is still 6 cm with routine outpatient follow-up
options.rationale: Oxytocin worsens compression by contracting uterus; the immediate need is delivery by category-1 caesarean unless immediate vaginal birth is possible. (Source: RANZCOG Umbilical cord prolapse statement)

options.text: Apply Kielland forceps to expedite vaginal delivery from -2 station with pudendal block only with standard supportive measures alongside
options.rationale: Instrumental delivery requires the head at or below the ischial spines with cervix fully dilated; -2 station at 6 cm is not amenable. (Source: RANZCOG Umbilical cord prolapse statement)

options.text: Perform emergency symphysiotomy in the birth suite while awaiting the anaesthetist to arrive with standard supportive measures alongside
options.rationale: Symphysiotomy is not part of the AU cord prolapse pathway; category-1 caesarean is the definitive management. (Source: RANZCOG Umbilical cord prolapse statement)

options.text: Elevate the presenting part manually and place her in knee-chest or exaggerated Sims position with a filled 500 mL bladder catheter and IV tocolysis if delivery is likely delayed
options.rationale: RANZCOG cord prolapse pathway uses manual elevation, positioning to relieve compression, bladder filling and tocolysis while transferring urgently to theatre for delivery. (Source: RANZCOG Umbilical cord prolapse statement)

explanation.summary: Cord prolapse is a category-1 obstetric emergency requiring delivery within 30 minutes (target 15 to 20). The immediate holding measures are: (1) manually elevate the presenting part with two fingers in the vagina to relieve cord compression, keep the fingers in place during transfer if possible; (2) position the mother in knee-chest, exaggerated Sims or Trendelenburg; (3) fill the bladder with 500 mL warmed saline via Foley catheter (raises the presenting part when manual elevation cannot be maintained); (4) start IV tocolysis (nifedipine or terbutaline) if delivery is likely to be delayed. Vaginal delivery is only pursued if the cervix is fully dilated with the head at or below spines. Category-1 caesarean is otherwise definitive. The cord should be kept warm and moist without excessive handling; do not attempt to reposition it above the cervix.
key_points: Manual elevation of presenting part is first-line during transfer.
Bladder filling with 500 mL saline relieves compression when hands must be freed.
Tocolysis buys time if there is any transfer delay.
Category-1 caesarean is definitive unless immediate vaginal delivery is possible.
explanation.pearls: In cord prolapse elevate the presenting part manually, fill the bladder with 500 mL saline, position in knee-chest and give tocolysis; deliver by category-1 caesarean within 30 minutes unless the cervix is fully dilated and head is at or below spines.

stem:
You are the O and G registrar in a metropolitan tertiary hospital. A 34-year-old woman (G4P3) delivered a 4.3 kg baby 45 minutes ago after a spontaneous labour induced for postdates. She had a manually removed placenta for retained placenta. Her booking bloods showed normal Hb and platelets. She has ongoing haemorrhage now totalling 2500 mL despite: Syntocinon 10 unit IM at delivery, Syntocinon 40 unit infusion running, ergometrine 250 microgram IM after 15 minutes, carboprost 250 microgram IM after 25 minutes, misoprostol 800 microgram PR, tranexamic acid 1 g IV, bimanual compression, empty bladder, and 2 units of packed cells running.

Her uterus remains soft and above the umbilicus. Speculum inspection is negative for genital tract trauma. Coagulation testing 10 minutes ago showed fibrinogen 1.9 g/L (2.0-4.5), platelets 78 x10^9/L, INR 1.4, temperature 35.4 degrees C. Consultant is 15 minutes away. Theatre is available now.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 132/min, blood pressure 84/48 mmHg, respiratory rate 26/min, SpO2 97 percent on 6 L oxygen, temperature 35.4 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Uterus soft, 2 cm above umbilicus; no visible genital tract trauma on speculum; bladder empty via IDC
data_table.Investigations: Fibrinogen 1.9 g/L (2.0-4.5); platelets 78 x10^9/L; INR 1.4; venous lactate 4.6 mmol/L; running 2 units PRBC

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step now?

options.text: Transfer to theatre for intrauterine balloon tamponade with continued transfusion and activation of massive transfusion protocol
options.rationale: RANZCOG PPH management escalates to mechanical tamponade (Bakri balloon) after pharmacological failure while blood product resuscitation continues; MTP activation covers ongoing coagulopathy. (Source: RANZCOG PPH statement; National Blood Authority MTP)

options.text: Repeat carboprost 250 microgram IM every 15 minutes until 8 doses are given regardless of hypertension
options.rationale: Carboprost is capped at 8 doses in total but tone-directed pharmacological therapy has already failed here; mechanical measures are indicated. (Source: RANZCOG PPH statement)

options.text: Repeat tranexamic acid 1 g IV every 30 minutes without other escalation until bleeding stops as the sole intervention
options.rationale: A second TXA dose is given at 30 minutes if bleeding continues, but escalation to mechanical and surgical measures should not be delayed. (Source: RANZCOG PPH statement)

options.text: Immediate hysterectomy in the birth suite without prior balloon tamponade or interventional radiology
options.rationale: Hysterectomy is definitive but is generally preceded by balloon tamponade or uterine compression sutures; jumping to hysterectomy skips reversible mechanical measures. (Source: RANZCOG PPH statement)

options.text: Continue current transfusion at the current rate and observe for another 30 minutes before further action
options.rationale: Ongoing haemorrhage above 2 litres with hypotension and coagulopathy requires immediate escalation, not observation. (Source: RANZCOG PPH statement)

explanation.summary: In refractory PPH after full pharmacological uterotonic escalation (oxytocin, ergometrine, carboprost, misoprostol), the RANZCOG pathway moves to mechanical measures - intrauterine balloon tamponade (Bakri, Rusch or Foley) - with concurrent blood product resuscitation. Massive transfusion protocol should be activated for ongoing losses above 40 percent blood volume with hypotension or coagulopathy; NBA guidance uses 1:1:1 ratios of PRBC, FFP and platelets with early cryoprecipitate if fibrinogen falls below 2 g/L. Warm the patient (hypothermia worsens coagulation). If balloon tamponade fails, surgical options are B-Lynch or other compression sutures, then internal iliac artery ligation or uterine artery embolisation, then hysterectomy as the definitive step. Balancing correction of the four Ts (tone, trauma, tissue, thrombin) continues throughout.
key_points: After pharmacological failure move to balloon tamponade with continued transfusion.
Activate MTP for >40 percent blood volume loss with hypotension or coagulopathy.
Cryoprecipitate is added early when fibrinogen falls below 2 g/L.
Hysterectomy is the definitive final step if mechanical and other surgical measures fail.
explanation.pearls: After maximal uterotonic therapy fails in PPH, transfer to theatre for intrauterine balloon tamponade with concurrent massive transfusion protocol activation, cryoprecipitate replacement of low fibrinogen, active warming and preparation for surgical compression sutures.

stem:
A 42-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder has been on lithium carbonate 750 mg nocte for 3 years with excellent mood stability. She attends your general practice for her scheduled review. Her most recent 12-hour post-dose lithium level 6 months ago was 0.7 mmol/L (target 0.6-0.8). She reports no polyuria or polydipsia and no fine tremor. She takes no other psychotropic medications.

She is asymptomatic today. Weight is stable at 68 kg (BMI 24 kg/m2). She has no personal or family history of thyroid disease, no cardiac history, and no NSAID use. Her booking bloods on lithium initiation showed normal renal function, thyroid function, calcium, and ECG.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 74/min, blood pressure 122/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert; no tremor; no goitre palpable; euthymic mood
data_table.Investigations: Recent lithium level 0.7 mmol/L 6 months ago (target 0.6-0.8); no bloods today yet

lead_in: What is the appropriate monitoring schedule at this visit?

options.text: Substitute lithium level with 24-hour urinary lithium excretion every 3 months as the sole intervention
options.rationale: 24-hour urinary lithium is not routine practice; standard is 12-hour post-dose serum level. (Source: RANZCP CPG Bipolar disorder)

options.text: Serum lithium level, urea and electrolytes, and thyroid function testing every 6 months in stable maintenance
options.rationale: RANZCP and eTG lithium monitoring in stable maintenance is lithium level, U and E, and TFTs every 6 months, with calcium annually and ECG when clinically indicated. (Source: RANZCP CPG Bipolar disorder; Australian eTG Psychotropic - Lithium)

options.text: Serum lithium level and renal function annually only in stable long-term maintenance
options.rationale: Annual monitoring is insufficient in maintenance; 6-monthly bloods including lithium level, U and E and TFTs are the standard. (Source: RANZCP CPG Bipolar disorder)

options.text: Full monitoring panel weekly for 4 weeks then no further testing for 12 months if stable
options.rationale: Weekly bloods are for initiation and dose change; long-term maintenance uses 6-monthly monitoring. (Source: RANZCP CPG Bipolar disorder)

options.text: Random lithium level and random calcium testing only in the presence of symptoms as the sole intervention
options.rationale: Routine 6-monthly scheduled monitoring detects subclinical thyroid or renal impairment before symptoms develop. (Source: RANZCP CPG Bipolar disorder)

explanation.summary: Long-term lithium monitoring per RANZCP and eTG in stable maintenance uses 6-monthly serum lithium (12 hours post-dose), U and E, and thyroid function tests, plus annual calcium level and clinically directed ECG. Baseline before initiation is renal function including eGFR, TFTs, calcium, ECG in patients over 40 or with cardiac risk, and a pregnancy test in women of reproductive age. Monitoring frequency increases with dose change, symptoms, or intercurrent illness (dehydration, NSAID use, ACE inhibitor initiation) that raises toxicity risk. Long-term lithium can cause nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, chronic kidney disease, hypothyroidism (up to 20 percent) and less commonly hyperparathyroidism. Target maintenance level in bipolar is 0.6 to 0.8 mmol/L.
key_points: 6-monthly lithium level, U and E, TFTs in stable maintenance.
Annual calcium and clinically directed ECG.
Baseline renal, thyroid, calcium, ECG, and pregnancy test where relevant.
Long-term risks include NDI, CKD, hypothyroidism, hyperparathyroidism.
explanation.pearls: For a stable long-term lithium patient the 6-monthly schedule is 12-hour post-dose lithium level, U and E and TFTs, with calcium annually; watch for hypothyroidism which affects up to 20 percent.

subtopic_detail: Smoking cessation pharmacotherapy in a depression comorbidity
stem:
A 48-year-old man presents to your general practice wanting to quit smoking. He smokes 20 cigarettes a day, has smoked since age 18, and has failed two prior quit attempts using patches alone. He has a history of moderate major depressive disorder currently well controlled on sertraline 100 mg daily for 2 years. He has no history of cardiovascular disease, no seizure history and no active suicidal ideation.

He drinks alcohol socially (5 standard drinks a week). His BMI is 27 kg/m2 and his blood pressure is 132/82. He has never used bupropion or varenicline. He asks for the option most likely to help him quit for good this time.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78/min, blood pressure 132/82 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert, euthymic; no clubbing; chest clear
data_table.Investigations: Recent fasting lipids and BSL within normal limits; PHQ-9 = 4

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Fluoxetine 20 mg daily instead of sertraline to help both mood and smoking cessation as the sole intervention
options.rationale: SSRIs are not evidence-based smoking cessation agents; his depression is already well controlled on sertraline. (Source: RACGP Supporting smoking cessation)

options.text: E-cigarettes (vaping) as monotherapy from the local vape store without prescriber involvement as the sole intervention
options.rationale: AU regulation of nicotine e-cigarettes now requires prescription and TGA-regulated products; unregulated vaping is not first-line pharmacotherapy. (Source: RACGP Supporting smoking cessation)

options.text: Varenicline titration starting at 0.5 mg once daily for 3 days, then 0.5 mg twice daily for 4 days, then 1 mg twice daily for 12 weeks
options.rationale: RACGP smoking cessation guidance places varenicline as first-line pharmacotherapy for adults; safety in stable depression is now well established. (Source: RACGP Supporting smoking cessation)

options.text: Bupropion sustained-release 150 mg once daily titrated to twice daily as sole pharmacotherapy as the sole intervention
options.rationale: Bupropion is an alternative but is contraindicated in seizure risk and less effective than varenicline; it is not preferred when varenicline is available. (Source: RACGP Supporting smoking cessation)

options.text: Nicotine 21 mg/24 hour patch alone applied daily without any oral pharmacotherapy as the sole intervention
options.rationale: Single-agent NRT has failed twice previously; escalation to varenicline or combination NRT is indicated. (Source: RACGP Supporting smoking cessation)

explanation.summary: The RACGP smoking cessation guideline uses the 5As framework and recommends behavioural support plus pharmacotherapy for adults smoking daily who want to quit. First-line pharmacotherapies are varenicline, combination NRT (patch plus a short-acting form) or bupropion; head-to-head evidence favours varenicline for quit rates, with combination NRT as a close second option. Varenicline safety in stable depression is now supported by the EAGLES trial data. Bupropion is contraindicated in seizure disorders, eating disorders, and MAOI use. Behavioural support (Quitline referral, motivational interviewing) is recommended alongside pharmacotherapy.
key_points: Varenicline is first-line pharmacotherapy for smoking cessation in Australian guidance.
Combination NRT is a close second when varenicline is unsuitable.
Bupropion is contraindicated in seizure risk and eating disorders.
Varenicline is safe in stable depression per EAGLES data.
explanation.pearls: For an adult smoking 20 a day who has failed NRT alone and has stable well-controlled depression, varenicline titrated to 1 mg twice daily for 12 weeks is first-line and does not require SSRI change.
